newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Theft at the top over the top, say S.Africa police.
newsitem.headline: Theft at the top over the top, say S.Africa police.

text.p: South Africa announced a crackdown on Wednesday to weed out light-fingered elements in the unit that guards cabinet ministers -- and apparently pinches their valuables as a sideline.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's gold watch, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki's hi-fi, Defence Minister Joe Modise's clock radio and Correctional Service Minister Sipo Mzimela's leather jacket were among items stolen recently, in a wave of crime that left no trace of forced entry.
Not to be outdone, Interior Minister Mangosuthu Buthelezi revealed to parliament this week that he too had been robbed -- at both his Cape Town and Pretoria homes.

"A compact disc player given to me by a friend in the United States was stolen in Cape Town and a big wall clock was stolen in Pretoria," he said, adding his name to the growing list of top-drawer victims.
Buthelezi said he also lost cutlery and a coffee table.

Some of the stolen goods were recovered last month when police raided the home of a member of the National Protection Service, the 2,000-strong special police unit that is supposed to look after VIPs.

For the struggling police force, battling one of the world's highest crime rates, the thievery has become embarrassingly bold. It comes on top of recent proof that corrupt policemen are involved in South Africa's industrial-scale car theft rings.

"This spate of thefts from the homes of the president, the deputy president and cabinet ministers necessitates urgent and incisive measures," the country's top police officer, Commissioner George Fivaz, said in a statement on Wednesday.
"This crime must be halted before it contaminates the reputation of the entire VIP protection component, the vast majority of whom are honest and hardworking officials."
Fivaz said random screening of National Protection Service members would begin immediately, including psychological examination and lie-detector tests.

The "personal cirmcumstances" of the modestly paid force would also be examined and there would be an inquiry into the whole structure of that part of the force responsible for simply guarding homes, rather than personal bodyguards.
"All known incidents fall within this sub-component," the statement said pointedly.

South Africans, however, have developed something of a Gallic shrug when it comes to police vows to stamp out crime, especially when crime-busting operations announced with square-jawed fanfare fail to match expectations.
A hi-fi was stolen from President Nelson Mandela's guest house on his property a year ago, and a guard at the presidential residence was later charged with the theft.

Newspaper reports say it was Mandela's likely successor, Deputy President Mbeki, who finally jolted the police into action when he returned from official business last week to find he too had been "done".
